mcqs.question: A loop calls `shape.area()` over a list of `Circle`, `Square`, and later a newly-added `Pentagon`. Why doesn't the loop need to change when `Pentagon` is added?
options: Because the loop was never written against any specific shape type — it only depends on the `area()` contract, which any new shape can satisfy
Because `Pentagon` inherits the loop's code automatically
Because Java automatically regenerates loops when new classes are added
Because area calculations are cached at compile time for every possible shape
mcqs.explanation: The loop depends only on the shared `area()` contract, not on which concrete types exist, so any new type implementing that contract is picked up automatically — that's polymorphism's extensibility payoff. There's no such thing as loops inheriting code or compile-time caching of every future shape's area.

mcqs.question: What determines which of two overloaded methods, `print(Shape)` and `print(Circle)`, gets called for a given call site?
options: The runtime type of the object actually being passed, resolved when the call executes
The method whose parameter type has the shorter name
Whichever overload was declared first in the source file
The declared (compile-time) type of the argument expression at the call site
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution is a compile-time decision based on the declared type of the argument expression, unlike overriding which resolves at runtime based on the object's actual class. Declaration order and name length play no role in which overload the compiler selects.

mcqs.question: Mechanically, how does calling `shape.area()` on a `Shape`-typed reference actually reach the correct `Circle` or `Square` implementation at runtime?
options: The compiler embeds every possible implementation directly at the call site and picks one with an if-check
The object carries a hidden pointer to its class's vtable; the call follows that pointer to look up the actual function address for `area`
The runtime re-compiles the calling code every time the object's type changes
Java scans the whole class hierarchy at every call to find a matching method by name
mcqs.explanation: Each object carries a pointer to its class's virtual method table, and a virtual call follows that pointer to the correct slot's stored address — one indirection, not a hierarchy scan or a runtime recompile. This is also why virtual calls have a small, constant overhead compared to a direct, non-virtual call.

mcqs.question: Given overloads `print(Shape)` and `print(Circle)`, calling `print(shape)` where `shape` is declared as `Shape` but actually holds a `Circle` object — which overload runs?
options: `print(Circle)`, because the compiler inspects the object's actual runtime type
Both overloads run, in declaration order
`print(Shape)`, because overload resolution uses the declared type of the expression, not the runtime type of the object it holds
It fails to compile, because the call is ambiguous
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution happens entirely at compile time from the declared type `Shape`, so `print(Shape)` is selected regardless of what the object actually is at runtime — the compiler never looks at the runtime type for this decision. Overriding, not overloading, is what would use the runtime type.

mcqs.question: A `Vehicle` constructor calls an overridable `getDefaultSpeed()`, which `SportsCar` overrides to return `topSpeed * 0.9`. What happens when `new SportsCar()` runs?
options: `getDefaultSpeed()` correctly returns 90% of `topSpeed`, since overriding always uses the final field values
The call throws a `NullPointerException` in every language that supports inheritance
`SportsCar`'s override runs before `SportsCar`'s own constructor has set `topSpeed`, so it computes off an unset default value instead of the intended one
Java silently skips the override in this case and calls `Vehicle`'s own default implementation instead
mcqs.explanation: Base constructors run before the subclass's own constructor body, but virtual dispatch still finds the subclass override — so the override runs while `topSpeed` is still at its uninitialized default, producing a wrong result rather than an exception or a silent fallback to the base implementation. This is exactly why calling overridable methods from a constructor is unsafe.
